response.title: Measuring a Stream
response.passage: During a field trip, Maya's class studied a stream behind the town library. The guide asked the students to watch the water for a full minute before making notes. That first pause kept them from mistaking a brief splash for the stream's usual current. Several students then placed small leaves at the edge and timed how long they traveled. The results differed because rocks slowed some leaves while the center of the stream moved faster. To compare observations fairly, each group released its leaf from the same marked point. The teacher also checked that every stopwatch was reliable by comparing it with a classroom clock. Once the groups trusted their timing, their measurements became easier to compare. The class learned that a steady flow can still change around an obstacle. After lunch, a rain shower raised the water level and made the current stronger. This change showed why a single measurement could not describe the stream all day. Back at school, students used the morning and afternoon notes to make a simple chart. Their report warned future visitors to check conditions before entering the water.
